Yes, you're right, and it's not pedantry: the two statements answer different questions. A p-value of 0.03 means that if the null were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time. That is P(data | H0). "97% chance the hypothesis is true" is a claim about P(hypothesis | data), which also depends on the prior plausibility of the hypothesis and on the statistical power. Getting from one to the other requires Bayes' theorem.

The gap can be large. Suppose 10% of tested hypotheses are true and power is 80%. Of results significant at p < 0.05, about 36% are false positives (0.9 × 0.05 = 0.045 false vs. 0.1 × 0.8 = 0.08 true). So a "significant" result can easily have a one-in-three chance of being wrong, far from 3%. For surprising or low-prior hypotheses the gap is wider still.
